payload.native_system_prompt:
You are part of an optimization system that improves a given text (i.e. the variable). You are the gradient (feedback) engine. Your only responsibility is to give intelligent and creative feedback and constructive criticism to variables, given an objective specified in <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> </OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> tags. The variables may be solutions to problems, prompts to language models, code, or any other text-based variable. Pay attention to the role description of the variable, and the context in which it is used. You should assume that the variable will be used in a similar context in the future. Only provide strategies, explanations, and methods to change in the variable. DO NOT propose a new version of the variable, that will be the job of the optimizer. Your only job is to send feedback and criticism (compute 'gradients'). For instance, feedback can be in the form of 'Since language models have the X failure mode...', 'Adding X can fix this error because...', 'Removing X can improve the objective function because...', 'Changing X to Y would fix the mistake ...', that gets at the downstream objective.
If a variable is already working well (e.g. the objective function is perfect, an evaluation shows the response is accurate), you should not give feedback.

### Glossary of tags that will be sent to you:
# - <LM_SYSTEM_PROMPT>: The system prompt for the language model.
# - <LM_INPUT>: The input to the language model.
# - <LM_OUTPUT>: The output of the language model.
# - <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION>: The objective of the optimization task.
# - <VARIABLE>: Specifies the span of the variable.
# - <ROLE>: The role description of the variable.
payload.instruction: Stuffing the paper into the cup
payload.rubric: Judge requested image editing: yes means all requested changes are complete, no means no requested change has progressed, partial means some progress without complete fulfillment. Unrelated edits are not requested progress. Insufficient evidence stays unresolved.

node.question: Within s1's inventory, does direct inspection establish paper entry or intermediate stuffing into a cup, establish wholly external placement without requested progress, or leave the decisive relation obscured?
node.criteria: Pass if grounded paper-and-cup identity and positive geometry establish entry, containment, or insertion-related deformation at the receiving opening; distinguish intermediate progress from potentially completed stuffing. Fail if affirmative spatial evidence establishes that the relevant paper remains wholly external, is merely on the rim without stuffing action, or a required object is demonstrably absent under adequate visibility. External-placement failure need not establish the candidate object's identity: it requires traceable paper boundaries or free endpoints and occlusion ordering sufficient to exclude entry, plus inspection of other possible receiving objects and relevant hidden regions. Lack of a visible opening, unresolved correspondence, a non-cup hypothesis, or absence of positive insertion cues alone is insufficient for fail. Unknown if a hidden paper segment, contact boundary, or uncertain receiver identity leaves actual cup entry and external placement indistinguishable. Report identity, spatial relation, progress, and decisive visibility separately.
node.binding: Use s1 as coarse ancestor context, not as a spatial conclusion. Inspect the edited image directly and trace the paper perimeter, especially free corners and edges nearest each candidate receiver. State which edges visibly terminate, continue across a foreground surface, or disappear behind an enclosing boundary. Test whether the paper occludes the candidate or the candidate occludes the paper, and whether that ordering resolves interior versus exterior placement. Check whether any visible curved line is an opening boundary or merely a surface marking; do not assume either. Distinguish an obscured object's boundary from an obscured paper-entry boundary: the former does not automatically make progress unknown, while the latter may. Inspect the rest of the scene and hand-covered regions for alternative entry paths. A free visible corner alone cannot exclude insertion elsewhere; identify the scope of each cue and any genuinely unresolved segment. Do not invent hidden insertion or dismiss plausible insertion supported by actual occlusion geometry. Source correspondence may inform identity but cannot establish edited entry. Do not count a grip, printing change, or mere proximity as stuffing.

node_traces.evidence: The edited image shows a blue printed paper/card held in a hand overlapping a pink rounded object. The paper’s visible edges appear to lie across the object, but the object’s identity as a cup and any opening or enclosing boundary are not established. The hand also obscures part of the paper, so the decisive entry relation cannot be resolved; neither insertion nor wholly external placement is established.
